lesson.subtitle: Lesson 12 -- Handling Questions
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Renato Annunciato | Lesson 12 -- Handling Questions
phases: The Words of the Q and A

listenings.text: After every presentation I ask at least two questions, and I want to explain why, because a lot of people take it personally. The first question is almost always about the source of a number. Where did this come from? How was it calculated? I am not attacking the speaker. I am checking whether the speaker knows the business behind the slide. The second question is usually a hypothetical. What would happen if the market changed, or if your biggest client left? I do not expect a perfect answer. I want to see how the person thinks. The worst answer is a long one that avoids the question. The best answer is short: it repeats my question in one sentence, gives a direct answer, and stops. And if the speaker does not know, I would much rather hear that he will get back to me than a number that somebody invented on the spot.

The first time I took questions in English, I was not worried about the presentation. I was worried about the questions, because I could not prepare them. And the first one came very fast, with an accent I did not know. I understood maybe half of it. So I did something I had never done in Portuguese. I said, sorry, could you repeat the last part of the question? She repeated it, more slowly, and it was easy. Nobody in the room cared. The second thing I learned was to make my questions indirect when I needed something from a director. Instead of saying, when will you decide, I said, could you tell me when you expect to decide? It was the same question, but it sounded like a partner, not a supplier. And the third thing: write down every question you could not answer, and answer it by email the next day. That email did more for my reputation than the whole presentation.

extra_audio.text: So your question is whether the growth will continue next year. The short answer is yes. Off the top of my head, the ballpark figure is two more percentage points. I will check the exact number and get back to you by Friday.

reading.rtitle: Handling the Q and A -- Notes for Breakout Speakers
paras: In the breakout sessions in Boston, each speaker has ten minutes to present and ten minutes for questions. Most delegates prepare the first ten minutes carefully and the second ten not at all. This note is about the second ten minutes, which are often the part that the directors remember.

Listen to the whole question before you answer. If it is long or unclear, rephrase it: so your question is whether the growth will continue next year? This gives you three seconds to think, and it shows the room that you understood. If you did not understand, ask: could you tell me which region you mean? Nobody will think less of you for asking a speaker to clarify.

When you do not know the answer, say so, and give a ballpark figure only if you are reasonably sure. Then say when you will get back to the person, and do it. A speaker who says I will check and send it to you by Friday looks more reliable than one who invents a number.

Finally, do not dodge. Directors notice when a speaker answers a different question from the one they asked. If a question is hypothetical, answer it as a hypothetical. If it brings up a concern that you share, say that it is a fair point before you explain your view.
